Having re-read it, the structure is already clean and I'm not going to reshuffle it just to look busy. But there is **one genuine, well-recognized weakness remaining**: median-of-three resists the *common* worst cases (sorted/reverse), but it does **not** guarantee O(n log n) — crafted "median-of-three killer" inputs (Musser, 1997) still drive plain quicksort to O(n²) *time*. (Stack depth is already safe via recurse-on-smaller.)

The standard fix is **introsort**: cap the partition depth and fall back to heapsort when exceeded — which is exactly what C++'s `std::sort` and Java's dual-pivot sort do. That converts the worst case from O(n²) to a guaranteed O(n log n). That's a real, targeted hardening, not pattern-sprawl, so it's worth doing. I'll also make the heapsort helper package-private so the fallback path can be white-box tested directly.

Clean compile under `-Xlint:all`, all 19 tests pass, demo output unchanged.

## What I changed this iteration

I made **one targeted algorithmic hardening** rather than restructuring code that's already well-organized: converted the quicksort into a proper **introsort**.

- **`sortRange`** now carries a `depthLimit` of `2·floor(log₂ n)`. When a partition path exceeds it — the fingerprint of an adversarial "median-of-three killer" input — that sub-range falls back to **heapsort**.
- Added `heapSort` + `siftDown` for both the `int[]` and generic paths (package-private, so the fallback is unit-testable without needing to construct a brittle adversarial sequence).
- Added a `heapSortFallbackPath` test: 200 randomized windowed trials confirming the fallback sorts correctly and leaves elements outside `[low, high]` untouched.

**Why it matters:** median-of-three only fixes the *common* worst cases (sorted/reverse). It does not bound the worst case — crafted inputs still force plain quicksort to O(n²) *time*. Introsort makes the worst case a guaranteed **O(n log n)**, which is what `std::sort` and Java's own library sorts do. (Stack depth was already O(log n) from the prior iteration.)

## On stopping here

I want to be straight with you: the codebase is now at a solid, library-grade state — robust algorithm, clean separation (library / demo / tests), validation, conventions, 19 passing tests. The remaining "refactors" I could invent — pluggable pivot-strategy interfaces, a factory, a DI/observer layer (the kind of thing the stale `ServiceRegistry`/`DIContainer` `.class` artifacts in this directory suggest a prior experiment did) — would be **over-engineering a sorting routine**, not improving it. I'd be adding indirection and surface area with no real payoff.

So I'd recommend stopping here unless you have a specific direction in mind (e.g., "make it stable," "add `long[]`/`double[]` overloads," "package it under a namespace with a build file").
